clips.title: Saudi Arabia is no richer per person than in 1990 #Shorts
clips.desc: The average American's output rose by three quarters. The average Saudi's didn't move.

clips.title: Kuwait was richer than America. Then this happened #Shorts
clips.desc: Output per person, adjusted for prices: almost $80k in 2006, about $48k in 2025.

clips.title: Kuwait pumps the same oil as 2005. With twice the people #Shorts
clips.desc: IMF oil output and World Bank population data.

clips.title: Same oil, opposite result: Norway vs Saudi Arabia #Shorts
clips.desc: Norway's oil fund: about NOK 3.8 million for every person.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $)
shots.narration: In 1990, the average American produced about forty-four thousand dollars of value a year, adjusted for prices and inflation. {p} The average Saudi? {pp} About sixty-five thousand. About one and a half times as much. {p} Thirty-five years later, the American number has climbed to about seventy-seven thousand. {p} And the Saudi number? {pp} About sixty-three thousand. {p} A little less than in 1990.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $)
shots.narration: And Saudi Arabia is the lucky one. {p} Kuwait. The Emirates. Qatar. Oman. {p} Some of the richest countries on Earth, sitting on some of its biggest oil reserves, where citizens pay no income tax. {p} Every one of them now produces less per person than it did at its peak. {pp} Kuwait, almost forty percent less.

These countries pumped oil, built cities out of the desert, and became a byword for wealth. {p} So how did they get poorer per person while most of the world got richer? {p} The answer is partly oil, partly people, {p} <soft>and partly a trick of arithmetic that makes the whole picture misleading.</soft>

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $)
shots.narration: Take Kuwait. {p} In 2006, the average Kuwaiti produced almost eighty thousand dollars a year, adjusted for prices. {p} About a third more than the average American. {p} By 2025, about forty-eight thousand. {pp} Down almost forty percent. {p} Today, it's less than two-thirds of the American level.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $)
shots.narration: The Emirates are even stranger. {p} In 1990, the average person there produced two and a half times as much as the average American. {p} Since then, Dubai has built the world's tallest building and one of its busiest airports. {p} And output per person has fallen by more than a third. {pp} Today it's a little below the American level.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $) · change from each country's peak to the latest year
shots.title: Below the peak
shots.narration: Qatar is still one of the richest places on Earth, at about a hundred and ten thousand dollars per person. {p} But that's about a quarter below its 2011 peak. {p} Oman, a quarter below its 2009 peak. {p} Brunei, in Southeast Asia, a third below 1991. {p} The exception is Bahrain, which depends less on oil and is now at an all-time high. {pp} Oil made these countries rich. <soft>It didn't keep them getting richer.</soft>

shots.src: IMF crude oil production, Kuwait (FRED KWTNGDPMOMBD)
shots.title: Kuwait's crude oil output
shots.narration: So what happened? {p} Start with the oil itself. {p} In 2005, Kuwait pumped about two point six million barrels a day. {p} In 2024, about two point four million. {pp} Roughly the same. {p} But the number of people sharing it went from about two point two million to about four point nine million. {pp} More than double.

shots.src: IMF, global price of Brent crude, annual average (FRED POILBREUSDA)
shots.narration: Why so many people? {p} Between 2003 and 2008, the price of oil more than tripled. {p} Gulf governments spent the windfall on airports, stadiums, malls and entire new cities. {p} To build and run them, they brought in workers. {pp} Millions of them. {p} Then, in 2014, the price crashed. Today it's about forty percent below its 2012 peak.

Across the Gulf, populations exploded. {p} Since 1990, Kuwait's population has almost tripled. {p} The Emirates', multiplied by six. {p} Qatar's, by almost seven: from about four hundred forty thousand people to almost three million. {p} The economies grew fast too. Qatar's is about five times bigger than in 2000. {pp} But when the population grows faster than the economy, output per person falls.

shots.src: IMF crude oil production, Saudi Arabia (FRED SAUNGDPMOMBD) · World Bank WDI (population 2000) · GAStat (population 2024)
shots.title: Saudi oil per person
shots.narration: Saudi Arabia shows the same math. {p} In 2000, it pumped about eight million barrels a day, for about sixteen million people. {p} In 2024, about nine million barrels, for more than thirty-five million people. {pp} About half as much oil per person.
Quick favor: if you're enjoying this, hit subscribe. It's free, and it's genuinely what keeps this channel going. {p} Now, the twist. {pp} Most of those new people aren't citizens.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · international migrant stock, % of population (UN DESA)
shots.narration: Today, about three in four people living in Qatar and the Emirates were born abroad. {p} In Kuwait, about two in three. In Saudi Arabia, about two in five, which is still about fifteen and a half million foreign residents. {p} They came to build the towers, staff the hospitals, drive the taxis and clean the homes.

shots.src: PACI / CSB Kuwait, population by nationality, 31 Dec 2024 (via GLMM) · Kuwait Central Statistics Administration, average monthly wages (via AGBI, 19 Mar 2025)
shots.title: Kuwait, end of 2024: 4.9 million residents

kicker.text: Citizens earn ~4.5× what foreign employees earn

shots.narration: Kuwait counts its people carefully. {p} At the end of 2024, it had about four point nine million residents. {p} Only about one point six million were Kuwaiti citizens. {p} The other three point three million were foreign residents, plus stateless people known as the Bidoon. {p} Roughly two non-citizens for every citizen. {p} And Kuwaiti citizens earn, on average, about four and a half times as much as foreign employees.

So when you divide Kuwait's economy by everyone who lives there, you're averaging a citizen's salary with a cleaner's. {p} Add millions of low-paid workers, and the average can fall even if nobody's pay goes down. {p} It's like a company whose average salary drops because it hired a thousand interns. Nobody took a pay cut. {pp} It's the mirror image of Ireland, where GDP per person is inflated by money that isn't really Irish.

shots.src: IMF crude oil production, Kuwait (FRED KWTNGDPMOMBD) · PACI / CSB Kuwait, population by nationality, 31 Dec 2024 (via GLMM)
shots.title: Oil per Kuwaiti citizen (barrels a day)
shots.narration: But even counting only citizens, the oil is stretched thinner. {p} Since 2005, the number of Kuwaiti citizens has grown by more than half. {p} In 2005, each citizen had about two point six barrels a day behind them. By 2024, about one point five. {p} Oil output per citizen is down about forty percent. {pp} The average is misleading. <soft>But the squeeze is real.</soft>

shots.src: PACI Kuwait, employment by sector and nationality, 30 Jun 2026 (via Kuwait Times, 23 Jul 2026)
shots.title: Who works where in Kuwait, mid-2026
shots.narration: And look at who does what. {p} By the middle of 2026, about four in five working Kuwaitis were employed by the state. {p} Only the rest worked for private companies, where more than ninety-six percent of the workforce is foreign. {p} The oil money pays the citizens. <soft>Imported workers run most of everything else.</soft>

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $)
shots.narration: But it's not just arithmetic. Compare Norway. {p} It pumps oil and gas too. {p} In 1990, the average Norwegian produced less than the average Saudi. {p} Since then, Norway's number is up about two-thirds, to about ninety-five thousand dollars a year. {p} Its population, now about five and a half million, grew by about a third, not six-fold. {pp} Same resource. Opposite result.

shots.src: Norsk Petroleum, Management of revenues (fund value end-2025); NBIM (first transfer 1996; ~1.5% of listed companies)
shots.title: Norway's oil fund
shots.narration: The difference is what Norway did with the money. {p} Since 1996, it has moved its oil income into a fund invested abroad, and the government may spend only the expected real return, about three percent a year. {p} Today the fund owns, on average, about one and a half percent of every listed company on Earth. {p} At the end of 2025, the fund was worth about twenty-one trillion kroner. {pp} About three point eight million kroner for every person in Norway.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · oil rents, % of GDP (NY.GDP.PETR.RT.ZS) · Kuwait Investment Authority
shots.narration: Gulf states have big funds too. Kuwait's, set up in 1953, is often called the oldest in the world. {p} But oil is a far bigger slice of their economies. {p} In 2012, oil rents were worth more than half of Kuwait's entire economy. In Norway, less than seven percent. {pp} Norway saved its oil. <soft>The Gulf built with it.</soft>

shots.src: Saudi Ministry of Human Resources (HRSD), Progress of the Saudi labor market (Dec 2025) · GASTAT Labour Force Survey Q1 2025 (via Argaam, 29 Jun 2025)
shots.title: Saudi women in the labor force
shots.narration: Saudi Arabia is trying to change the math. {p} Since 2016, its Vision 2030 plan has pushed citizens into jobs once filled by foreigners. {p} The share of Saudi women in the workforce has more than doubled, from seventeen percent in 2017 to about thirty-six percent in early 2025. {p} And unemployment among Saudi citizens hit a record low of about six percent, beating the plan's target of seven. {p} That's part of why its output per person is now back near its 1990 level, after two decades well below it.

But the clock is ticking. {p} Nobody knows exactly when the world's demand for oil will stop growing. {p} Saudi Arabia, the Emirates and Qatar are racing to build tourism, finance and tech industries before that day comes. {p} Some of it is working. Much of it is still paid for by oil. {p} When demand does stop growing, the countries that saved will be fine. {pp} The ones that spent will need a new answer to an old question: <soft>what happens to a country when the oil stops paying?</soft>

next.title: Ireland is the richest country in Europe

shots.narration: To see the opposite trick, where GDP per person makes a country look far richer than it is, watch my video on Ireland. {p} I'm Chartbound. See you in the next one.

yt.title: Saudi Arabia Is No Richer Than in 1990
yt.description:
In 1990 the average Saudi produced about 1.5 times as much as the average American, adjusted for prices. Today, a little less than in 1990, while the American number rose by three quarters. Kuwait is almost 40% below its 2006 peak; the Emirates more than a third below 1990. Why the Gulf's oil states got poorer per person: the same oil shared by far more people, averages that mix citizens with millions of low-paid migrant workers, and the country that did it differently, Norway.

Sources: World Bank WDI (NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD, SP.POP.TOTL, NY.GDP.MKTP.KD, SM.POP.TOTL.ZS, NY.GDP.PETR.RT.ZS, ); Saudi Ministry of Human Resources (HRSD, Dec 2025) and GASTAT Labour Force Survey; IMF crude oil production via FRED (KWTNGDPMOMBD, SAUNGDPMOMBD); PACI/CSB Kuwait population by nationality (via Gulf Labour Markets, Migration and Population programme); GAStat Saudi Arabia (population 2024); Kuwait Central Statistics Administration wages (via AGBI, March 2025); Norsk Petroleum and NBIM (Government Pension Fund Global); Kuwait Investment Authority.
